items.content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.

items.title: GRAD: Graph-Structured Antibody Defense for LLM Agents
items.author: Tianqi Song, Jiawei Du, Xuemei Jia, Zheng Wang
items.content: Memory poisoning and decomposition attacks distribute malicious evidence across the operations of large language model agents. Existing request-level defenses can miss such attacks because they assess individual inputs without connecting earlier information to later actions. Moreover, detectors must adapt as task contexts change, while updates to shared parameters can impair previously learned detection capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose GRAD, which combines graph-based evidence aggregation across operations with an extensible collection of detection experts. Its Semantic-Structural Understanding Module (SSUM) jointly encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed candidate relations in an execution graph to aggregate distributed attack evidence into a graph-level risk score. Its Continual Antibody Adaptation (CAA) adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures, acquiring and reusing detection capabilities as tasks arrive. Across Decomp, MCP, and MRT, GRAD achieves AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60%, respectively, outperforming Sequential Monitor and locally adapted Agent-Sentry and NeuroTaint. CAA improves final accuracy by 13.08 percentage points over Replay on the cross-dataset task stream. The gain remains 9.05 points with equal family/base-case weights within each task. Its compact drop-in gate performs local model inference in milliseconds without monitoring API calls.

items.title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
items.author: Mayank Arya, Agrim Bari, Anjaly Parayil, Yogesh Simmhan, Renee St. Amant, Victor R\"uhle, Saravan Rajmohan
items.content: Agentic large language model (LLM) applications turn one user request into a sequence of model and tool calls over a growing context. Retaining this context's key-value (KV) state in GPU memory lets later calls reuse it instead of recomputing it, but at fleet scale this needs substantial memory. We characterize four production Microsoft M365 workload traces (Deep Research, Enterprise Assistant, Coding Agent and Enterprise Chat) spanning more than 121 million model calls. In Deep Research, the application issues 89% of model calls and the median context grows from about 10K to 68K tokens by the 30th call. About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache. With the public Llama-2-70B KV layout standing in for confidential models, one 99th-percentile Deep Research session exceeds the 80 GB HBM of an NVIDIA H100, and holding all live sessions at their peak needs an estimated 501.8 TB of HBM, although inference occupies only 5.6% of that retention time. Trace-driven replay shows that a one-hour idle cap cuts this ceiling by 3.6x while raising the share of calls that recompute context only from 4.07% to 4.53%. Under tighter budgets, eviction alone is insufficient: at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute and clairvoyant furthest-next-use 31%, whereas multi-resolution retention (MRR), which demotes the LRU session's KV state to int4, lowers this to 13.6%. Placement imposes a separate limit: when the next call reaches a different deployment, cached-context reuse drops from 89% to 29%, and treating KV state as deployment-local raises the recompute floor under unlimited memory from 5.4% to 20.2%. These findings motivate retention that changes the representation of KV state, together with deployment-aware routing or migration. We plan to release AgenticTraceSim, a parametric trace generator, and a residency replay framework.
